title: IOC Clears Path for Russia at LA 2028, but Flag and Anthem Still in Limbo
summary:
In a move that could reshape the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics, the International Olympic Committee (IOC) has provisionally lifted its suspension of the Russian Olympic Committee (ROC). The decision, announced Tuesday, marks a significant shift toward ending Russia’s sporting isolation — but key symbols of national pride remain off the table for now.

The ROC was suspended in October 2022, eight months after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, for recognizing regional Olympic councils in four Ukrainian territories occupied by Russia: Luhansk, Donetsk, Kherson, and Zaporizhia. The IOC deemed this a violation of the Olympic Charter and Ukraine’s territorial integrity. Now, the IOC says the ROC has confirmed it no longer includes those regional bodies as members and will not conduct activities there. “The decision was taken following a thorough analysis by the IOC’s Legal Affairs Commission,” the IOC stated.

IOC President Kirsty Coventry addressed the controversy head-on. “We don’t condone any wars, including this one. We will continue to support Ukraine like we have since this started. But I don’t believe athletes should pay the price,” she said. “We don’t want to hold athletes accountable for the actions of their government.” She added that the IOC will closely monitor Russia and reserves the right to take further measures.

Russian athletes have competed as neutrals — without their flag, colors, or anthem — at the 2024 Paris Summer Games and the 2026 Milano Cortina Winter Games. Whether that changes for LA 2028 remains undecided. Russian Sport Minister Mikhail Degtyarev celebrated the move as “a green light for international federations to reinstate all our athletes.” Ukraine has not yet responded.

The decision unfolds against the backdrop of Russia’s state-sponsored doping scandal, which led to a ban from competing under its flag at multiple Olympics. Coventry emphasized the need for rigorous drug testing of Russian athletes heading into LA28.

This provisional lifting doesn’t guarantee a full return. The IOC’s executive board will continue to monitor the situation, and any misstep could trigger renewed sanctions. For now, the door is open — but the flag remains folded.
why_it_matters: For teens who dream of competing internationally, this case shows how politics can shape an athlete's ability to represent their country, raising questions about whether sports should be separate from government actions and what fairness truly means on a global stage.

background_read: The International Olympic Committee (IOC) is the Switzerland-based organization that runs the Olympic Games and decides which countries can take part.

Russia's sports isolation began long before the 2022 Ukraine invasion. After the 2014 Sochi Games, it was revealed that Russia ran a state-sponsored doping program. As a result, Russian athletes could not compete under their own flag at the 2018 Pyeongchang Winter Olympics, the 2020 Tokyo Summer Games, and the 2022 Beijing Winter Games. Instead, they competed as 'ROC' (Russian Olympic Committee) or 'neutral' athletes.

The Olympic Charter (the rulebook of the Olympic movement) says that no country may violate the territorial integrity of another. When Russia officially recognized sports councils in four Ukrainian regions it occupied, the IOC suspended the ROC in October 2022.

Kirsty Coventry, a former Olympic swimmer from Zimbabwe who won seven medals, became the first woman and first African to lead the IOC. She must now balance calls for accountability against the desire to include all athletes worldwide.

The 2028 Los Angeles Games will be the first Summer Olympics held in the United States since 1996. The IOC's decision is provisional, meaning the door is open for Russia but could close again if it makes a misstep.

perspectives.description: Athletes who had no role in their government's actions can return to international competition, promoting individual fairness and the Olympic ideal of bringing the world together through sport. Many young Russians have trained for years and deserve a chance to compete.

Critics argue that lifting the suspension too early rewards Russia and weakens the consequences for violating international law and the Olympic Charter. It might signal that occupying another country's territory can be forgiven if enough time passes, undermining the IOC's rules.

Olympic boycotts and exclusions have been used as diplomatic tools for decades (like the US-led boycott of the 1980 Moscow Games), but their long-term effectiveness in changing state behavior is debated. The IOC routinely walks a tightrope between universal participation and ethical standards, and this is just the latest chapter.

The IOC's provisional approach means Russia must continue to comply, but the unresolved anthem and flag issue could spark future tensions or even athlete boycotts. Future Olympic host selections may also face pressure to exclude nations involved in conflicts, making geopolitics impossible to ignore.
